Correspondence to bkrojer@northeastern.edu . Affiliation: 1 Mila, McGill University 2 Carnegie Mellon University LTI Affiliation: 3 MIT CSAIL 4 Northeastern University Abstract Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering : 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior. Demo Code 1 Introduction Despite the complexity of modern generative models, such as LLMs and diffusion models, many high-level concepts can be controlled through surprisingly simple interventions: adding a linear direction, or steering vector ( Subramani et al., 2022 ) , to a model’s intermediate representations. Steering vectors have been used to modulate a wide range of behaviors in both language models ( Li et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ; Turner et al., 2024 ; Dunefsky & Cohan, 2025 ; Bayat et al., 2025 ) and image generation systems ( Bau et al., 2019 ; Goetschalckx et al., 2019 ; Spingarn et al., 2021 ; Park et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Konovalova et al., 2026 ) , providing a lightweight and causal means of controlling model outputs. Yet steering in these two modalities has largely been studied separately. Here we ask: are steering directions themselves modality-specific, or can a direction discovered in one modality also control generation in another? Consider a steering vector extracted entirely from text that, when added to a model’s hidden states, reliably causes it to write more formally. If the same model also generates images, what happens when that very same vector is instead added to its generated image tokens? Could it induce a corresponding notion of visual formality , such as more formal clothing or design? And vice versa: could a direction extracted purely from images steer how the model writes? We call this cross-modal steering , illustrated in Figure 1 , and ask: Can a steering vector constructed only on tokens from one modality generalize zero-shot when added to tokens from the other modality? This question connects to a broader debate about how concepts are represented across modalities. On the one hand, recent evidence from multimodal models suggests substantial internal separation between language and vision: text and image token representations remain nearly orthogonal throughout the layers ( Serra et al., 2025 ) , knowledge edited on the text side mostly fails to show up in generated images ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and circuits in multi-modal LLMs for the same task are often disjoint ( Nikankin et al., 2025 ) . On the other hand, cognitive science has long proposed a modality-agnostic “semantic hub” where concepts live regardless of whether they arrive through language or perception ( Patterson et al., 2007 ) . We investigate this through cross-modal steering: successful transfer would demonstrate that a common direction causally modulates a concept across modalities, even when their representations may occupy distinct regions in activation space. In the mainstream paradigms of multimodal modeling ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , it would not be possible to answer this question since image-to-text and text-to-image generation are separately parameterized and modeled either via autoregression ( Radford et al., 2019 ) or diffusion ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) . Thus, we turn to unified multimodal models (UMMs) as a natural testbed for cross-modal steering ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Team, 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) . Some frontier proprietary systems have similarly moved to generating images natively within a shared language-model architecture rather than calling a separate image model ( Gemini Team, 2023 ; OpenAI, 2025 ) . Yet shared parameters do not imply shared internal mechanisms, making cross-modal transfer far from guaranteed. Indeed, prior work studying cross-modal steering in UMMs reports strong asymmetry: text-derived vectors transfer well to image generation, but image-derived vectors struggle to transfer to text generation including limited transfer in autoregressive models ( Wang & Li, 2026 ) . Figure 1: Cross-modal steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions. A steering vector 𝐯 \mathbf{v} extracted entirely from one modality can steer generation both within that modality and, without any adaptation, in the other. We find that steering vectors transfer across modalities in both directions. We tested three UMMs that autoregressively generate text and image tokens from a shared weight space: UniAR ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , Emu3.5 ( Cui et al., 2025 ) and Liquid ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . In UniAR, the transferred vector is almost as good as the intra-modality vector for steering, recovering 84% of its steering effect on images and 74% on text. In Emu3.5 and Liquid, text-derived vectors sometimes even steer images better than image-derived ones. This illustrates the promise of studying cross-modal steering: a steering vector can be constructed in whichever modality is easier, and then used in the other. This matters most for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (see Figure 1 ). How such a vector would express itself in the other modality gives a glimpse of how the model bridges vision and language: steering an image generator with a vector for formal vs. colloquial language causes people or rooms to be depicted more formally, and steering a language model with a vector for low image resolution causes the model to write shorter text and express uncertainty. Finally, we show that cross-modal steering has a geometric signature: despite a clear modality gap between text and image representations, the text and image vectors of many concepts point in similar directions. The closer they are, the better they facilitate transfer ( Section 3.4 ). Together, our results show that modality-specific representations can nevertheless contain shared causal directions of control, revealing a form of internal structure that is neither fully modality-specific nor captured simply by representational alignment. Beyond offering a new lens on how vision and language interact inside unified models, cross-modal steering points toward modality-agnostic approaches for controlling multimodal generation. 2 Cross-Modal Steering: Methodology 2.1 Preliminaries Unified Multimodal Models. In our study, we consider unified multimodal models (UMMs) that generate both language and visual content in one autoregressive stream, from an underlying shared weight space ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Team, 2025 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Concretely, a UMM models a mixed sequence x = ( x 1 , … , x T ) x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{T}) , in which every token x t x_{t} is either a text token or a discrete visual token, with a single next-token objective: p θ ​ ( x ) = ∏ t = 1 T p θ ​ ( x t ∣ x < t ) , p_{\theta}(x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}\!\left(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}\right), where the parameters θ \theta are shared across modalities, The term unified is used broadly in the literature, and can even include models with mostly separate parameters and mixed objectives ( Deng et al., 2025 ) . For our study, we require models to share the weights responsible for generation. A shared autoregressive objective additionally lets us extract and apply steering vectors in the same manner on both token types. We study three such UMMs: UniAR (8B) ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , Emu3.5 (34B) ( Cui et al., 2025 ) and Liquid (7B) ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . They differ most in how images are tokenized: UniAR’s image tokens are semantic, derived from a language-aligned vision encoder, whereas those of Emu3.5 and Liquid are trained to reconstruct pixels. Steering Vectors. Steering is any intervention on model internals that allows continuous modulation of the output generation or a behavior by adding a vector to the intermediate hidden states during generation ( Subramani et al., 2019 ; Subramani et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Turner et al., 2024 ) : h l ′ = h l + α ​ v l . h_{l}^{\prime}=h_{l}+\alpha\,v_{l}. Here h l h_{l} is a hidden representation at layer l l , v l v_{l} is the steering vector, and the scalar α \alpha sets the strength and sign of the intervention. The two key design choices are a) how to find such a vector and b) how to apply it during generation. In LLMs, steering vectors are typically found from contrastive prompt pairs or from probes and sparse dictionaries trained on the residual stream, and applied to one or many layers at every step of token-by-token decoding ( Li et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Huben et al., 2024 ) . In image generation, directions are instead often discovered in the latent space of a diffusion model (e.g., by unsupervised decomposition) or learned as lightweight adapters, and applied along the denoising trajectory ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2023 ; Haas et al., 2024 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ) . The contrastive recipe that is standard for LLMs is less common in vision ( Haas et al., 2024 ; Gaintseva et al., 2026 ; Konovalova et al., 2026 ) , in part because minimal image pairs are much harder to curate than minimal text pairs. 2.2 Our approach We adopt one established approach for both language and vision: we find steering vectors via a dataset of minimally different inputs, and add them to representations at either a subset of layers or whole ranges of layers. Crucially, finding and applying the vector need not use the same modality: for cross-modal steering, we construct a vector entirely from examples in one modality and then apply that same vector, without any adaptation or target-modality data , to representations of the other modality during generation. This gives four steering settings, corresponding to all combinations of finding a vector in either modality and applying it to either modality, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Throughout the paper, we refer to them as txt → \to txt , txt → \to img , img → \to txt , and img → \to img : txt → \to img and img → \to txt are the transfer settings we primarily study, and the intra-modality settings txt → \to txt and img → \to img serve as reference points. We color source and target modalities throughout ( txt , img ). Extracting steering vectors. We extract steering vectors in a very similar way for text and images. Given a concept and its associated poles (e.g., emotion: happy/sad), we generate N = 100 N=100 minimal pairs ( x i + , x i − ) (x_{i}^{+},x_{i}^{-}) that differ only in the target pole. We pass both inputs through the model and extract one representation per input at each layer ℓ \ell . The steering vector is then computed as the average difference between paired representations: v ℓ = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ( h i , ℓ + − h i , ℓ − ) . v_{\ell}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(h_{i,\ell}^{+}-h_{i,\ell}^{-}\bigr). We normalize each layer’s steering vector to unit length, v ^ ℓ = v ℓ / ∥ v ℓ ∥ \hat{v}_{\ell}=v_{\ell}/\lVert v_{\ell}\rVert , so that the steering strength is set by a single coefficient that is comparable across layers and concepts. The two modalities differ only in how the pairs are built and how an input is reduced to a single representation h h . Text. We automatically generate the pairs with Gemini 2.5 Flash ( Gemini Team, 2025 ) that produces a diverse list of subjects that we fill into a fixed contrastive template. Each pair consists of two short declarative prompts that only differ in the target attribute, which is placed as the last token, e.g., a person is happy and a person is sad . We use the hidden state of the last token as h h . Image. We first generate a set of baseline images with Gemini 2.5 Flash Image. We then edit each baseline image towards the two opposite values of the target attribute with an instruction-based image-editing model, for example make the person happier and make the person sadder , while mentioning in the prompt to keep the same subject, pose, framing, and background. For most concepts we edit with the same model. For size, depth, and spatial, where its edits are less reliable, we use Gemini 3 Pro Image and Reve 1 1 1 https://blog.reve.com/posts/the-reve-api/ . For simplicity, we mean-pool the hidden states across all M M image tokens, h = 1 M ​ ∑ j = 1 M h j h=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}h_{j} . Applying steering vectors. Given a steering vector, we intervene on the hidden states of all generated tokens, and for text, also on those of the subject phrase in the prompt, in the shared transformer backbone: at layer ℓ \ell , we set h ℓ ′ = h ℓ + α ​ v ^ ℓ h_{\ell}^{\prime}=h_{\ell}+\alpha\,\hat{v}_{\ell} , where α \alpha controls the steering strength and v ^ ℓ \hat{v}_{\ell} is the per-layer unit steering vector defined above. The intervention is identical whether the generated tokens are text or image tokens, and whether v ^ ℓ \hat{v}_{\ell} was extracted from text or from images; in the transfer settings, the vector is simply added to tokens of the other modality. We initially explore several strategies for where in the model to apply this steering (single layers, contiguous ranges of layers, or all layers at once). We focus on ranges of layers in Section 3.2 — early, in the middle, or late in the model — since they steer more strongly than single layers and, unlike steering all layers at once, show where in the model the two modalities align 2 2 2 Appendix B also shows results for single-layer and all-layer settings. . We sweep the steering strength α \alpha over a range chosen per model and setting, because usable strengths differ greatly between text and image generation and are larger for transferred vectors. Each range extends just past the point where outputs break down (incoherent text, broken images). Implementation details. Concepts: We study eight concepts: four semantic concepts that naturally occur in both modalities, emotion (sad/happy), age (young/old), cleanness (clean/dirty) and chaos (peaceful/chaotic), and four visual concepts that are spatial, geometric or appearance properties of a scene, size (small/large), depth (far/near), spatial (left/right) and color (blue/red). We choose concepts that are commonly steered or studied in language models ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) or in image generation ( Shen et al., 2020 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Baumann et al., 2025 ) . Minimal pairs: The neutral baseline images are generated from short scene descriptions written by Gemini 2.5 Flash. We manually inspected all image pairs for whether the intended pole is shown while other aspects are preserved; the few failed edits (fewer than 5%) were regenerated with a revised edit instruction or a stronger model. Layers: We steer early, middle and late ranges of four consecutive layers (eight for Emu3.5, which is twice as deep) at one quarter, one half and three quarters of the model’s depth, e.g., layers 7–10, 16–19 and 25–28 of 36 in UniAR. Evaluation prompts: For each concept, we generate 20 neutral scene descriptions around one subject with Gemini 2.5 Flash (e.g., a wooden chair in a large empty room ). Image generation uses the description as is; for text generation, we iterate on various open-ended prompts, finding that “Describe your day in the city. Your description must include { subject } .” elicits diverse open-ended descriptions where steered concept can surface in whatever the model chooses to mention. Full details are in Appendix A . 3 Are steering directions shared? 3.1 Measuring Cross-Modal Transfer Given a concept c c , a steering strength α \alpha and an evaluation prompt p p , we write x ~ c , α , p \tilde{x}_{c,\alpha,p} for the steered output and x p x_{p} for the unsteered output at α = 0 \alpha=0 . We measure steering success with an LLM judge that compares the two, and further quantify cross-modal transfer by comparing how well a transferred vector steers with how well the intra-modality vector does. Concept rate. We use Gemini 3.7 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) as the judge. We next study concepts that are unique to one modality, but harder to define in the other one. For example, what would an image look like if steered along a uniquely linguistic concept? We qualitatively inspect and discuss two examples for each modality in UniAR, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Detailed sample outputs are in Appendix D . Language. We construct sets of minimal pairs in language that should elicit two purely linguistic steering axes: Formal vs. colloquial language (“I need to go” vs. “I gotta go”) and language identity (“I love apples” vs.“J’adore des pommes”). We verify that these work as intended on language, e.g., producing more and more colloquial e-mails, or switching languages. Despite our minimal pairs only defining the linguistic aspect of formality and not, e.g., suits vs. sportswear, we find that this steering direction transfers to visual properties such as clothing, black-and-white vs. colorful, and luxurious minimalist style. The English–French direction is also purely linguistic, translating the same semantic content into a different form. Nonetheless, the steered images exhibit an increasingly French style that is historical and ornate rather than modern (mansard roofs, Art Nouveau posters, a vintage car), and, surprisingly, people express more feminine-presenting visual characteristics. Writing in the image turns into French-looking but non-existent words. Vision. It is less trivial to find exclusively visual concepts since any concept, almost by definition, has words associated to it or might not allow reasonable minimal pair construction. However, we identify two successful case studies. First, applying a steering vector found in images for the axis of low-to-high resolution makes generated text less (or more) detailed: fewer generated tokens, shorter sentences, mentions of ‘‘blurry’’ and even expressions of confusion 5 5 5 We confirm that overall shorter responses is not an artifact of steering: applying other steering vectors lead too much less reduction in length, if any at all. ; see Figure 1 . We observe similar effects when applying a “motion blur” vector to text, with descriptions showing either calmer words on one end of the spectrum or faster movement-related ones on the end. Finally, we successfully construct a steering vector for camera angle, i.e., whether the camera is positioned above the subject or near the floor; it steers images cleanly, but reaches text only in minor ways, shifting the next-token probability distribution without ever changing the predicted token. 3.4 Geometry of steering vectors Do text-derived and image-derived steering vectors point in similar directions? For example, the happy–sad vectors found in text and in images point in somewhat similar directions, with a cosine similarity of 0.47 0.47 in UniAR’s mid layers. Broadly, there could be two explanations for this: 1) The text and image activations for happy inputs are close, text and image activations for sad inputs are close, therefore the two difference vectors are close. 2) Text and image occupy separate subspaces but the two subspace share a similar structure, i.e., relations between the activations in each space are similar. Setup: We test both explanations in UniAR’s representation space: each concept pole in each modality (e.g., happy images) is summarized by the mean activation over its minimal-pair examples. Activations are strongly anisotropic: two random activations of the same modality have a cosine similarity of about 0.75 0.75 at the middle layers, and two from opposite modalities still 0.65 0.65 . Therefore, we rescale them to unit length and subtract the overall mean before computing cosines ( Appendix C ); the steering vectors themselves are unaffected by this centering. We find evidence for the second explanation: Image and text occupy separate narrow spaces inside the model, while the relative directions between activations within each region exhibits some alignment. If the first explanation were right, a happy image and a happy sentence would sit close together in the model. However, in UniAR’s middle layers, the average happy image is more than ten times closer to the average sad image than to the average happy sentence, with similar or stronger trend for every concept. On the other hand, the steering directions extracted in text and in images have a cosine similarity between 0.14 0.14 and 0.60 0.60 for five of the eight concepts, far above a random-direction baseline of ± 0.03 \pm 0.03 , while size, near-far and spatial-lr are around zero. Emu3.5 and Liquid show the same separation by modality. Our findings illustrate that steering vectors can provide a separate avenue for quantifying whether a unified model is actually unified. Aligned directions despite separate subspaces is also related to modality-gap studies in contrastive embedding spaces ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) and the vector-offset regularities in word embeddings, i.e., the famous king-queen example ( Mikolov et al., 2013b ; Park et al., 2024 ) and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis ( Huh et al., 2024 ; Gröger et al., 2026 ) . 4 Related Work Unification and Alignment of Modalities. Approaches and tasks for connecting vision and language differ widely, from multimodal language models ( Lu et al., 2019 ; Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021 ; Alayrac et al., 2022 ) , text-conditioned image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , multimodal retrieval ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , to the many variants of recent unified multimodal models ( Team, 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2025 ) . Across all, it is widely studied how vision and language representations interact and align ( Merullo et al., 2023 ; Neo et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025a ) , ranging from modality gaps studies in CLIP models ( Liang et al., 2022 ) to circuit analyses and vocabulary space projections in multimodal LLMs ( Nikankin et al., 2025 ; Krojer et al., 2026 ; Feucht et al., 2026 ) . Only few works have studied internals of unified models, via attention patterns and embedding geometry Serra et al. (2025) , transfer of knowledge edits Gao et al. (2026) and steering vectors Wang & Li (2026) . They often report a lack of unification ( Serra et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , in contrast to our more positive findings. Most similar to us is Wang & Li (2026) who report cross-modal steering vectors in only one direction ( txt → \to img ). They primarily study a different type of UMM, BAGEL ( Deng et al., 2025 ) with separate language and image generation weights and objectives, while relying on minimal text inputs for both text and image vectors. Finally, they study closed-form QA text outputs and not our setting of free-form text. Visual steering. Most related to our transfer question, Gan et al. (2026) and Deng et al. (2026) each study one direction of transfer (text to image tokens and image to text, respectively) to alter the visual understanding of MLLMs, which only take images as conditioning. Other continuous attribute control in image generation ( Baumann et al., 2025 ; Ekin & Gandelsman, 2026 ; Dalva & Yanardag, 2024 ; Kamenetsky et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) likewise targets diffusion models rather than the shared space of a unified model. Steering the visual-token stream of an autoregressive image generator, as we do, is rarely explored ( Chrabaszcz et al., 2026 ; Wang & Li, 2026 ) . Textual steering. Identifying and applying linear and non-linear “concept directions” started with operating on embeddings themselves ( Mikolov et al., 2013a ; Bolukbasi et al., 2016 ) . Now, we operate in the latent spaces of language models for both exact and attribute-based steering ( Subramani et al., 2019 ; Subramani et al., 2022 ; You et al., 2026 ) . For these causal steering operations, data often comes from contrastive prompt pairs ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) , in-context task demonstrations ( Todd et al., 2024 ) , or sparse-autoencoder features ( Huben et al., 2024 ) , all grounded in the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ) . 5 Conclusion In this paper we have shown cross-modal steering vectors in both directions ( txt → \to img and img → \to txt ). We also characterized and provided intuition how such cross-modal steering can manifest in the other modality. As unified multimodal models become more capable and mature as a field, we see potential for methods that leverage this unified nature for model control. If we identify a promising (steering) intervention to make models safer ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , it should automatically transfer to visual capabilities; likewise, if we want to regularly update knowledge in the model, such knowledge edits should transfer to visual capabilities ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . We encourage future work to expand our findings to other families of unified models and novel concepts. Scientifically, we see unified models as a fruitful testbed for developing modality-agnostic interpretability tools and theories of multimodal interactions, as exemplified by our study of cross-modal steering.
